rationale: The book's core claim — that 'the heart of the earth' in Matthew 12:40 is Jerusalem, the navel/center of the land, rather than the tomb or Sheol — is supported by an actual scriptural lexical anchor that the common reading lacks. No supplied or cited text ever calls a grave 'the heart of the earth,' whereas Ezekiel 5:5 explicitly places Jerusalem 'in the midst of the nations,' Ezekiel 38:12 uses tabbur ha'aretz ('navel of the land,' the same word as Judges 9:37), and Jonah's own mirrored phrase bilvav yammim ('heart of the seas,' Jonah 2:3) — combined with the established symbol sea = peoples/nations (Revelation 17:15) — makes 'heart of the earth/land' read naturally as the land's center. The reading also dissolves the notorious chronological problem: counting from the arrest to the resurrection yields three days and three nights and matches Luke 24:21 ('today is the third day since these things were done'), whereas the Friday-burial-to-Sunday tomb reading cannot supply three nights without idiomatic special pleading or relocated crucifixion days. The strongest counter (tomb/Sheol) explains the descent imagery of Jonah 2 but explains nothing the book's reading cannot: Jesus' death and burial occurred within Jerusalem's custody and within the book's three-day span, and Jonah praying alive in the belly, 'as good as dead,' fits the custody reading at least as well as a literal death-realm reading. The counter, by contrast, cannot ground its identification in any text and inherits the counting problem the book resolves. On the supplied evidence, the book's identification is the better-supported explanation.
book_core_identification: 'The heart of the earth' (Matthew 12:40) is Jerusalem — the navel and heart of the land, the city God set 'in the midst of the nations' (Ezekiel 5:5; 38:12) — so the three days and three nights measure the Son of Man's time under Jerusalem's power from His arrest to His resurrection, not merely his interval in the tomb.
book_secondary_elaborations: The three-day count begins at the arrest outside the gates on the night of betrayal, not at burial, and ends the third day per Luke 24:21

The mirrored phrase 'heart of the seas' (bilvav yammim, Jonah 2:3), with sea = peoples (Revelation 17:15), identifies Jonah's destination as the center of the gentile world, making the two phrases parallel city-centers
The great fish is a devouring ruler (per Jeremiah 51:34; Ezekiel 29:3; 32:2), fulfilled in Caesar/Rome acting through Jerusalem ('We have no king but Caesar')
The scene-by-scene typology mapping Jonah's flight, storm, interrogation, casting, and Nineveh's repentance onto the betrayal, trials, crucifixion, resurrection, and gentile mission
Extra-biblical attestation: Philo ('heart of the whole earth'), the Sibylline Oracles ('navel and heart of the earth'), and later Greek Ezekiel copies reading 'heart' for 'navel'
The reeds (suph) about Jonah's head as the crown of thorns; 'Salvation (yeshuah) is of the LORD' as the name Jesus; mountains = kingdoms in Jonah 2:6
Nineveh's three days' journey read as three thousand years via 2 Peter 3:8
strongest_counter_interpretation: 'The heart of the earth' refers to Jesus' burial in the tomb and, in the fuller traditional form, his sojourn in Sheol/Hades, the realm of the dead beneath the earth: Jonah in the fish's belly cried 'out of the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2), went down to 'the bottoms of the mountains' with 'the earth with her bars' about him, and was brought up 'from corruption' — language Peter applies to Christ's grave via Psalm 16:10 (Acts 2:27-31). On this reading the analogy is confinement in death: as Jonah was as-good-as-dead in the deep, so the Son of Man would be dead and buried in the earth before rising the third day, with Ephesians 4:9 ('the lower parts of the earth') and the burial narratives (Matthew 27:57-60) supplying the referent.
counter_core_identification: The heart of the earth is the grave/tomb and the subterranean realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades) in which Jesus lay between death and resurrection.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that 'the heart of the earth' is Jerusalem or any above-ground location: it insists the phrase denotes the place of the dead entered only at death and burial, so the three days and three nights begin at the entombment, not the arrest — the two identifications assign different referents and different starting points to the same measured interval and cannot both be true.
counter_case: Jonah's own prayer glosses the fish's belly as 'the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2), suggesting the antitype is the death realm, not a city
'I went down to the bottoms of the mountains; the earth with her bars was about me' (Jonah 2:6) is descent-into-the-earth imagery, matching a subterranean referent for 'heart of the earth'
'Thou hast brought up my life from corruption' (Jonah 2:6) is the very language Peter applies to Christ's body in the grave (Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27-31), tying the Jonah type to entombment
The downward spatial force of 'heart of the earth' (kardia tēs gēs) parallels 'the lower parts of the earth' (Ephesians 4:9) in the traditional descent reading
The sign's climax is death and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3-4: 'buried... raised the third day'), and the burial narratives supply a concrete referent for where Jesus spent the interval
This is the overwhelming consensus reading across traditions (70%+ per the book's own survey), placing the burden of proof on the novel identification
book_explanatory_advantages: It supplies actual scriptural warrant for the identification: Ezekiel 5:5 ('This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations') and Ezekiel 38:12 (tabbur ha'aretz, 'navel of the land,' same word as Judges 9:37), whereas no text ever calls a grave 'the heart of the earth'

The mirrored phrase in Jonah's own prayer — bilvav yammim, 'the heart of the seas' (Jonah 2:3, flattened by the KJV) — combined with the defined symbol sea = peoples/nations (Revelation 17:15) yields a symmetrical reading: heart of the seas = center of the gentile world; heart of the earth/land = center of the land = Jerusalem

It resolves the chronological problem the tomb reading created: arrest Thursday night to resurrection Sunday yields three days and three nights, and matches Luke 24:21 exactly, without idiomatic partial-day counting or Wednesday-crucifixion proposals

It absorbs rather than denies the counter's data: Jesus' death, burial, and Sheol descent all occur within His time under Jerusalem's power, and Jonah praying alive in the belly ('as good as dead') fits custody-unto-death better than literal residence among the dead

The fish-as-devouring-ruler symbol is independently established in Scripture (Jeremiah 51:34 of Nebuchadnezzar, 'swallowed me up like a dragon'; Ezekiel 29:3; 32:2 of Pharaoh; Jeremiah 51:44, 'I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed'), making the swallowing-and-giving-back a coherent political-resurrection figure

Contemporary usage corroborates: Philo calls Jerusalem the 'heart of the whole earth' and the Sibylline Oracles 'the navel and heart of the earth,' showing the phrase was a live designation of Jerusalem in Jesus' world

It explains why Luke's version says Jonah himself 'was a sign' (Luke 11:30) — the whole lived story, not one entombment clause — which the extensive scene-for-scene Passion parallels then substantiate
counter_explanatory_advantages: Jonah 2's Sheol, corruption, and bars-of-the-earth language most naturally evokes the death realm, and Acts 2:27-31 canonically links that language to Christ's grave
The tomb/Hades reading is the near-universal traditional interpretation, requiring no symbolic apparatus (sea = nations, fish = ruler) to run
The spatially downward sense of 'heart of the earth' parallels Ephesians 4:9 without remainder
It keeps the analogy simple: fish's belly = confinement in death; heart of the earth = confinement in death
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 5:5 — God's own identification: 'This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations'
Ezekiel 38:12 — tabbur ha'aretz, 'the navel of the land' (with Judges 9:37 using the same term for the country's center)
Jonah 2:3 — bilvav yammim, 'the heart of the seas,' the mirrored phrase anchoring the parallel
Revelation 17:15 — 'the waters... are peoples, and multitudes, and nations,' the defined symbol that converts 'heart of the seas' into 'center of the nations'
Luke 24:13,21 — 'to day is the third day since these things were done,' fixing the count the book's reading satisfies
Matthew 12:40 — the primary text, whose 'three days and three nights' the tomb reading cannot fill from a Friday burial
Philo and the Sibylline Oracles — first-century attestation of Jerusalem as the 'heart of the earth'
Jeremiah 51:34,44 — the swallowing ruler forced to give back, grounding the fish-as-kingdom symbol
unresolved_objections: Jonah 2's Sheol/corruption language, applied to Christ in Acts 2:27-31, retains genuine pull toward a death-realm sense that the book subsumes but does not eliminate
Hebrew idiom may allow 'three days and three nights' as inclusive reckoning of partial days, which would weaken the chronological advantage claimed for the Jerusalem reading
Golgotha and the tomb lay technically outside the city walls, so 'in Jerusalem' must be construed as 'under Jerusalem's power/jurisdiction' rather than strictly within the walls
The extra-biblical witnesses (Philo, Sibylline Oracles, revised Greek Ezekiel copies) are corroborative, not scriptural proof, as the book itself concedes

Secondary elaborations in the chapter — the day-as-a-thousand-years reading of Nineveh's three days' journey, and the deferred full calendar case — are speculative and were not weighed as part of the core
